strengths: Compelling and practical motivation: eliminating the reliance on active depth sensors or offline, pre-built 3D reconstructions (e.g., SfM, NeRF, 3DGS) by integrating an end-to-end feed-forward 3D reconstruction model (CUT3R) directly into a video-language model.

Well-designed architecture: using latent geometry and camera pose tokens from a continuous 3D reconstructive model and fusing them with 2D visual tokens via cross-attention provides a lightweight yet effective 3D grounding mechanism without dealing with irregular raw point clouds.

Valuable benchmark and data contribution: curating over 200K spatial QA instances and proposing VSTemporalI-Bench (138.6K QA pairs) helps fill an important gap in assessing spatial-temporal dynamics (such as camera displacement and relative motion) over time.

Thorough ablation study (Table 3): isolates the impact of the newly generated dataset versus the architectural components by comparing against a fine-tuned baseline ('LLaVA-NeXT-Video ft w/o C&G Tok'), confirming the positive impact of both geometry and camera tokens.
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparisons in main tables: In Table 1, VLM-3R is compared directly against zero-shot / out-of-the-box foundation models (LLaVA-NeXT-Video at 35.6 vs. VLM-3R at 60.9). However, Table 3 reveals that fine-tuning the base model on the 200K data alone yields 57.74. While the additional +3.16 boost from 3D tokens is valid, Table 1 obscures how much of the performance jump stems from task-specific SFT versus 3D representation.

Evaluation protocol on VSTemporalI-Bench (Table 2): The manuscript states that VLM-3R was fine-tuned on the VSTI-Bench training split (132.5K QA pairs), while other open-source models appear to be evaluated zero-shot. Comparing an in-domain fine-tuned model against zero-shot baselines leads to an unbalanced comparison; providing a fine-tuned 2D baseline (e.g., fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video) on VSTI-Bench would make the comparison much more rigorous.

Generalization and scope: The evaluation is restricted to static indoor datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes). There is no investigation into potential catastrophic forgetting on general video VQA benchmarks, nor evidence of how the model performs in outdoor or dynamic object settings.

strengths: Compelling and practically motivated direction: Operating directly on monocular RGB videos without requiring explicit depth maps, active sensors (e.g., LiDAR), or pre-built 3D meshes solves a major bottleneck in scaling 3D-aware vision-language models for real-world robotics and egocentric video applications.

Well-designed architecture: Rather than ingesting raw, unstructured point clouds, VLM-3R innovatively leverages implicit geometric features and camera pose/view tokens from a modern feed-forward 3D reconstruction foundation model (CUT3R), effectively bridging 2D visual representations and metric 3D scene structure via cross-attention.

Comprehensive dataset and benchmark contribution: The automated spatio-temporal scene-graph curation pipeline generates over 200K spatial instruction-tuning pairs and introduces VSTemporalI-Bench (138.6K QA pairs) to specifically test dynamic, temporal-spatial reasoning (camera displacement, ego-motion direction, evolving camera-object distances).

Detailed ablation studies: The ablations in Table 3 cleanly isolate the specific contributions of the curated data, camera tokens, and geometric tokens, showing that both geometry and camera tokens provide concrete empirical gains beyond pure 2D fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison on VSTemporalI-Bench (Table 2): VLM-3R is fine-tuned on the massive 132.5K VSTI-Bench training split, whereas general-purpose baselines (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5, LLaVA, InternVL2) appear to be evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning on this domain-specific data. An apples-to-apples fine-tuned baseline (e.g., fine-tuning LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B on the same VSTI training set) is missing in Table 2.

Disentangling data scaling from architectural innovation on VSI-Bench: In Table 1, VLM-3R jumps to 60.9% compared to base LLaVA-NeXT-Video at 35.6%. However, Table 3 reveals that simply fine-tuning LLaVA-NeXT-Video on the 200K spatial data accounts for the vast majority of this leap (achieving 57.74%), with the 3D geometry/camera tokens contributing an additional +3.16%. While +3.16% is a solid gain, the paper text occasionally overstates the architectural impact versus the data curation impact.

Lack of evaluation on general video understanding benchmarks: Fine-tuning on 200K domain-specific spatial/navigation QA pairs risks catastrophic forgetting of broader video comprehension capabilities. The authors should evaluate VLM-3R on standard video QA/LMM benchmarks (e.g., Video-MME, MVBench, or ActivityNet QA) to test whether general perception and reasoning are preserved.

Missing runtime, latency, and memory analysis: Running a recurrent transformer-based dense 3D reconstructor (CUT3R) frame-by-frame alongside a standard 2D vision backbone (SigLIP) adds notable inference overhead. Quantitative metrics regarding inference latency (FPS/latency per video sequence) and GPU VRAM footprint during inference should be reported.

Minor presentation issues: In Section 3.2, 'Route Planing' contains a typo. In Appendix A.2, the manuscript mentions 'training was set for 5 epochs... but concluded after the first epoch' without clarifying why early stopping was applied (e.g., overfitting or compute constraints).

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: enabling 3D visual-spatial and spatio-temporal reasoning directly from monocular RGB video without requiring specialized depth sensors or pre-built 3D point cloud maps.

Sensible architectural integration: rather than attempting to ingest irregular 3D point clouds, the framework cleverly repurposes intermediate latent geometry and camera tokens from a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model (CUT3R) and fuses them with 2D visual tokens via cross-attention.

Comprehensive data contribution: curates a large-scale (200K+) spatial instruction tuning dataset and introduces VSTemporalI-Bench (138.6K QA pairs) targeting camera dynamics and evolving camera-object spatial relationships over time.
The paper is clearly structured and provides thorough implementation and dataset generation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Fairness of baseline comparisons in benchmark tables: In Table 1, baseline models (including proprietary APIs and open-source models) are evaluated zero-shot, whereas VLM-3R is instruction-tuned on 200K task-specific QA pairs. As revealed in the ablation study (Table 3), simply fine-tuning the base LLaVA-NeXT-Video model on the curated data raises its performance from 35.6 to 57.74, while adding the proposed 3D tokens and fusion only further improves it from 57.74 to 60.90. This indicates that most of the apparent margin over existing methods is driven by supervised fine-tuning data rather than architectural innovation.

Unbalanced setup on VSTemporalI-Bench: As noted on page 7, VLM-3R is fine-tuned on the VSTI-Bench training split (132.5K QA pairs), whereas baseline models (GPT-4o, Gemini, open-source models) appear to be evaluated zero-shot without fine-tuning on this training split. A fine-tuned baseline (e.g., fine-tuned LLaVA-NeXT-Video without 3D tokens) should be included in Table 2 to isolate the contribution of the architecture.

Limited evaluation domain and generalizability: Both the training data and benchmarks are constructed from the same indoor RGB-D datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes) in static scenes. The manuscript does not evaluate out-of-domain generalization or performance on in-the-wild dynamic videos with moving objects.

Potential risk of scene overlap / data leakage: The paper should explicitly clarify scene-level train/test splits between the newly generated 200K training QA dataset, VSI-Bench, and VSTemporalI-Bench to ensure no overlapping room scans exist across training and evaluation sets.

strengths: Addresses a key limitation in current 3D-VLMs: eliminating the dependency on explicit depth sensors or pre-built 3D point cloud maps by leveraging monocular video through a feed-forward metric-scale geometry encoder (CUT3R).

Effective architectural design: using both implicit spatial context tokens and camera view/motion tokens within a lightweight cross-attention residual fusion block (Spatial-Visual-View Fusion) instead of passing raw or heavy explicit 3D point clouds directly into the LLM.

Substantial benchmark and dataset contributions: curates a 200K+ spatial instruction tuning dataset (including 4,225 Habitat route-planning instances) and introduces VSTI-Bench with over 138K QA pairs specifically probing temporal spatial relationships induced by egocentric camera motion.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, OST-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OpenEQA), where VLM-3R achieves strong performance that rivals or exceeds depth-supervised and large video-language baselines.
Insightful ablation studies analyzing the distinct utility of spatial vs. view tokens, implicit token fusion vs. explicit point fusion, and comparing different geometric backbones (CUT3R vs. VGGT).
weaknesses: Dataset domain scope: Both the training curation and the proposed VSTI-Bench originate from the same underlying indoor scan datasets (ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes). While train/test scene splits are strictly respected, evaluating generalization to outdoor, dynamic, or unconstrained in-the-wild web videos is limited.

Disentangling data scaling vs. architectural gains: In Table 1, fine-tuning the base model on the 200K curated data already boosts performance from 35.6 to 57.7, while adding the 3D reconstructive tokens accounts for an additional ~3.2 points (reaching 60.9). A clearer discussion in the main text distinguishing the data-scale contribution from the architectural inductive bias would strengthen the presentation.

Inference and computational overhead: Running an end-to-end multi-view geometry model (CUT3R) alongside the standard visual backbone introduces additional latency and memory overhead. The paper lacks a quantitative runtime/FLOPs/FPS comparison between the base VLM and VLM-3R during multi-frame video inference.

Evaluation setup clarity on VSTI-Bench: The manuscript does not clearly state whether all open-source baselines in Table 2 are evaluated purely zero-shot, or whether any were fine-tuned on the VSTI-Bench training split.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical limitation in current video large multimodal models (LMMs): the absence of metric-scale geometric understanding from monocular video without relying on explicit depth sensors or brittle pre-built 3D point cloud pipelines.

The integration of implicit 3D tokens and camera view tokens from a feed-forward metric reconstruction model (CUT3R) via cross-attention is well-motivated and computationally cleaner than directly processing explicit, irregular 3D point clouds.

Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks (VSI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, and zero-shot OpenEQA) demonstrate consistent performance gains over both 2D video LMMs and competitive performance against models requiring explicit 3D/depth inputs.

The newly curated 200K spatial instruction-tuning dataset and the 138.6K QA-pair VSTI-Bench provide a valuable resource for diagnosing and improving camera-motion-induced spatio-temporal reasoning in multimodal models.
Ablation studies are thorough, comparing explicit point cloud fusion, ablation of spatial/view tokens, and alternative geometric foundation models (such as VGGT vs. CUT3R).
weaknesses: The evaluation and data curation are strictly restricted to static indoor environments (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes), meaning temporal dynamics are solely induced by camera trajectory rather than true scene dynamics (e.g., moving objects, human-object interactions).

There is an observed slight degradation in general visual QA performance (e.g., non-spatial questions in OpenEQA drop from 67.22% to 65.54%, and Video-MME drops from 62.7% to 59.9% without general video data mixing), indicating minor domain trade-offs / forgetting.
The technical novelty of the fusion module is relatively modest, relying on standard single-layer cross-attention and projection layers to fuse pretrained visual and geometric representations.

For the VSTI-Bench evaluation (Table 2), it is somewhat unclear whether the baseline open-source models were fine-tuned on the VSTI training split or evaluated in a zero-shot manner, which could confound the comparison against VLM-3R.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of current video Large Multimodal Models (LMMs): the lack of metric-scale 3D geometric awareness and spatial-temporal reasoning from monocular RGB video without relying on depth sensors or pre-computed SLAM point clouds.

Well-motivated model design that leverages implicit 3D tokens and camera view tokens from a metric-scale multi-view geometry foundation model (CUT3R) via cross-attention (Spatial-Visual-View Fusion), circumventing the irregularities and computational overhead of explicit point clouds.

Comprehensive data curation pipeline providing over 200K 3D reconstructive QA pairs and simulated route planning trajectories, complemented by the introduction of VSTI-Bench (138.6K QA pairs) targeting camera dynamics and spatio-temporal reasoning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VSTI-Bench, ScanQA, SQA3D, OST-Bench, and OpenEQA) showing consistent improvements over open-source baselines and competitiveness with methods utilizing ground-truth 3D/depth inputs.
weaknesses: The majority of the performance gain on VSI-Bench stems from the curated 200K instruction tuning dataset rather than the architectural module alone; fine-tuning the base model (LLaVA-NeXT-Video) on the data raises performance from 35.6% to 57.7%, while the 3D geometric token fusion contributes an additional +3.2% (to 60.9%).

Evaluation and dataset curation are restricted strictly to static indoor scenes (ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes), where scene dynamics arise solely from camera motion; dynamic objects and outdoor scenes are unaddressed.
A discrepancy exists in the text versus Table 6: the text in Section 5.3 states that without view tokens the score drops to 50.09, whereas Table 6 reports 59.09.
The computational overhead (inference latency, FLOPs, and GPU memory usage) of running the CUT3R geometry encoder alongside the primary vision backbone and LLM is not quantitatively analyzed.
